source_text: Quale autem spectaculum in proximo est aduentus domini iam indubitati, iam superbi, iam triumphantis! quae illa exultatio angelorum, quae gloria resurgentium sanctorum! quale regnum exinde iustorum! qualis ciuitas noua Hierusalem! at enim supersunt alia spectacula, ille ultimus et perpetuus iudicii dies, ille nationibus insperatus, ille derisus, cum tanta saeculi uetustas et tot eius natiuitates uno igni haurientur. quae tunc spectaculi latitudo! quid admirer? quid rideam? ubi gaudeam, ubi exultem, tot spectans reges, qui in caelum recepti nuntiabantur, cum Ioue ipso et ipsis suis testibus in imis tenebris congemescentes? item praesides persecutores dominici nominis saeuioribus quam ipsi flammis saeuierunt insultantes contra Christianos liquescentes? quos praeterea? sapientes illos philosophos coram discipulis suis una conflagrantibus erubescentes, quibus nihil ad deum pertinere suadebant, quibus animas aut nullas aut non in pristina corpora redituras adfirmabant? etiam poetas non ad Rhadamanthi nec ad Minonis, sed ad inopinati Christi tribunal palpitantes? tunc magis > tragoedi audiendi, magis scilicet uocales in sua propria calamitate; tunc histriones cognoscendi, solutiores multo per ignem;tunc spectandus auriga in flammea rota totus ruber; tunc xystici contemplandi, non in gymnasiis, sed in igne *** iaculati, nisi quod ne tunc quidem illos uelim uisos, ut qui malim ad eos potius conspectum insatiabilem conferre, qui in dominum desaeuierunt. hic est ille, dicam, fabri aut quaestuariae filius, . sabbati destructor, Samarites et daemonium habens; hic est quem a Iuda redemistis, hic est ille harundine et colaphis diuerberatus, sputamentis dedecoratus, felle et aceto potatus; hic est, quem clam discentes subripuerunt, ut surrexisse dicatur, hortulanus detraxit, ne lactucae suae frequentia commeantium adlaederentur. ut talia spectes, ut talibus exultes, quis tibi praetor aut consul aut quaestor aut sacerdos de sua liberalitate praestabit? et tamen haec iam quodammodo habemus per fidem spiritu imaginante repraesentata. ceterum qualia illa sunt, quae nec oculus uidit nec auris audiuit nec in cor hominis ascenderunt? credo, circo et utraque cauea et omni stadio gratiora.
thought_title: The coming spectacle of Christ's judgment
orientation: Tertullian is closing the treatise by contrasting the shows of this world with the far greater spectacle of Christ's return and final judgment, which Christians already possess in part through faith.
pass_a_gloss: But what a spectacle is near at hand: the coming of the Lord, now undoubted, now proud, now triumphant! What exultation of angels there will be, what glory of the saints rising again! What a kingdom of the just from then on! What a city, the new Jerusalem! But indeed other shows remain: that last and everlasting day of judgment, that day unhoped for by the nations, that day mocked, when so great an age of the world and so many of its births will be consumed by one fire. What breadth of spectacle then! What shall I admire? What shall I laugh at? Where shall I rejoice, where shall I exult, seeing so many kings, who were announced as received into heaven, groaning together with Jupiter himself and with their own witnesses in the lowest darkness? Likewise the governors, persecutors of the Lord's name, melting away amid flames more savage than those with which they themselves raged against Christians, insulting them? Who besides? Those wise philosophers blushing before their own disciples as they burn together with them, to whom they used to persuade that nothing pertains to God, to whom they used to affirm that souls are either nothing or will not return to their former bodies? And the poets, trembling not before the tribunal of Rhadamanthus nor of Minos, but before the tribunal of the unexpected Christ? Then the tragic actors will be more worth hearing, more vocal, of course, in their own calamity; then the actors will be worth recognizing, much more loosened by the fire; then the charioteer will be worth watching, all red on his flaming wheel; then the xystici (gymnasts trained in the covered training gallery) will be worth contemplating, not in the gymnasiums, but in the fire, hurled, except that not even then would I wish them to be seen, since I would rather direct an insatiable gaze toward those who raged against the Lord. This is he, I shall say, the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute, the destroyer of the Sabbath, a Samaritan and one having a demon; this is he whom you bought from Judas; this is he who was beaten with a reed and with blows, disgraced with spittle, given gall and vinegar to drink; this is he whom his disciples secretly stole away, so that it might be said that he rose, whom the gardener dragged away, so that his lettuces might not be damaged by the crowd of people passing through. To see such things, to exult in such things, what praetor or consul or quaestor or priest will provide them to you from his own generosity? And yet these things we already have in some way, represented through faith as the spirit imagines them. But what sort are those things which neither eye has seen nor ear has heard nor have they ascended into the heart of man? I believe they are more pleasing than the circus and both tiers of seats and every stadium.

choices.why: Standard rendering of aduentus for Christ's return; 'coming' preserves the noun's force rather than a verbal paraphrase.
rejected: the arrival of the Lord
the Lord's advent

choices.term: iam indubitati, iam superbi, iam triumphantis
choices.english: now undoubted, now proud, now triumphant
choices.why: The repeated 'iam' marks escalating certainty and exaltation; 'proud' keeps the Latin superbus, which here means exalted and glorious rather than arrogant.
rejected: now certain, now haughty, now victorious
already undoubted, already exalted, already triumphing

choices.why: The word order 'ciuitas noua Hierusalem' is appositional; rendering as 'the new Jerusalem' is natural English while preserving the noun ciuitas implicitly.
rejected: the city, the new Jerusalem
a new city, Jerusalem

choices.term: ille ultimus et perpetuus iudicii dies
choices.english: that last and everlasting day of judgment
choices.why: Perpetuus means 'everlasting' or 'never-ending'; 'everlasting' captures the eternal consequence of the judgment day.
rejected: that final and perpetual day of judgment
that last and endless day of judgment

choices.why: Insperatus means 'unhoped for' or 'unexpected'; the dative nationibus indicates for whom it is unexpected. 'Unhoped for' preserves the passive verbal idea.
rejected: unexpected by the nations
unhoped for among the Gentiles

choices.english: will be consumed by one fire
choices.why: Haurio means 'to swallow up, consume'; 'consumed' fits the image of fire devouring the world's age and births.
rejected: will be drained by one fire
will be swallowed by one fire

choices.english: who were announced as received into heaven
choices.why: The passive nuntiabantur indicates that these kings were publicly proclaimed or reported as having been received into heaven; 'announced' preserves the public declaration.
rejected: who were said to have been received into heaven
who were reported as taken up into heaven

choices.english: the governors, persecutors of the Lord's name
choices.why: Praesides refers to provincial governors who persecuted Christians; 'governors' is the standard rendering, and 'persecutors of the Lord's name' keeps the genitive phrase.
rejected: the magistrates, persecutors of the name of the Lord
the rulers who persecuted the Lord's name

choices.english: amid flames more savage than those with which they themselves raged
choices.why: The comparative saeuioribus flammis is ablative of means; the clause means the flames are more savage than the savagery they inflicted. 'Raged' preserves the verb saeuio.
rejected: in fiercer flames than they themselves raged with
by flames more cruel than their own cruelty

choices.why: Sapientes is ironic; 'wise' preserves the irony without adding commentary.
rejected: those so-called wise philosophers
those philosophers who thought themselves wise

choices.term: animas aut nullas aut non in pristina corpora redituras
choices.english: souls are either nothing or will not return to their former bodies
choices.why: The philosophers denied either the existence of souls or their return to the same bodies; 'former bodies' renders pristina corpora.
rejected: souls either do not exist or will not return to their original bodies
souls are either nothing or will not come back into their former bodies

choices.english: before the tribunal of the unexpected Christ
choices.why: Inopinatus means 'unexpected, unlooked for'; the poets did not expect Christ as judge. 'Unexpected' is the plain rendering.
rejected: before the tribunal of the unforeseen Christ
before the judgment seat of the unhoped-for Christ

bible_refs.note: quod nec oculus uidit nec auris audiuit nec in cor hominis ascenderunt

pass_b_english: But what a show is already near at hand: the coming of the Lord, now no longer doubted, now glorious, now triumphant! What exultation among the angels, what glory for the saints as they rise again! What a kingdom of the righteous will follow! What a city, the new Jerusalem! But there are still other shows to come: that last and everlasting day of judgment, unhoped for by the nations, the day they mocked, when all this world's great age and all its births will be consumed by one fire. What a vast spectacle that will be! What should I marvel at? What should I laugh at? Where should I rejoice, where should I exult, as I watch so many kings who were announced as received into heaven, groaning in the deepest darkness with Jupiter himself and with their own witnesses? And the governors, persecutors of the Lord's name, melting away amid flames more savage than those with which they themselves raged against the Christians? Who else? Those wise philosophers, blushing before their own disciples as they burn together with them—the ones who taught that nothing pertains to God, who insisted that souls are either nothing or will not return to their former bodies? And the poets, trembling not before the judgment seat of Rhadamanthus or Minos, but before the tribunal of the Christ they did not expect? Then the tragedians will be worth hearing, far more vocal in their own calamity; then the actors will be worth watching, much more loosened by the fire; then the charioteer will be worth seeing, all red on his flaming wheel; then the xystici will be worth contemplating, not in their gymnasiums but in the fire, hurled—except that I would not even then wish to look at them, since I would rather fix an insatiable gaze on those who raged against the Lord. This is he, I will say to the persecutors, whom you called the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute, the destroyer of the Sabbath, the Samaritan who is possessed by a demon; this is the one you redeemed from the Jews; this is the one beaten with a reed and with blows, disgraced with spittle, given gall and vinegar to drink; this is the one his disciples secretly stole away so that he could be said to have risen, the one the gardener dragged away so that his lettuces might not be damaged by the crowd of people passing through. What praetor or consul or quaestor or priest will grant you from his own generosity the chance to see such things, to exult in such things? And yet we already have these things in some way, represented through faith as the spirit imagines them. But what are those things which no eye has seen and no ear has heard, nor have they ascended into the heart of man (1 Corinthians 2:9)? I believe they are more delightful than the circus and both tiers of seats and every stadium.
notes: The text contains a lacuna marked by *** after 'in igne' before 'iaculati'; the missing word or words cannot be recovered from the source.

problems.quote: the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute
problems.why: Latin says 'son of a carpenter or of a tax‑collector', not a prostitute.
problems.fix: the son of a carpenter or of a tax‑collector
problems.ruling: quaestuariae means prostitute/harlot, not tax-collector (publicanus). Translator is correct; checker's claim is wrong.

edits.old: the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute
edits.new: the son of a carpenter or of a tax-collector

fixed: Changed 'prostitute' to 'tax-collector' for 'quaestuariae' (source: 'fabri aut quaestuariae filius').

problems.quote: the son of a carpenter or of a tax-collector
problems.why: quaestuaria means prostitute, not tax-collector; it's a stock pagan slur at Mary.
problems.fix: the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute
problems.ruling: ‘quaestuariae’ likely means ‘prostitute’, a slur, not ‘tax‑collector’; translation changes the intended polemical meaning.

problems.quote: the one you bought from Judas
problems.source_quote: hic est quem a Iuda redemistis
problems.why: ‘a Iuda’ means ‘from the Jews’, not ‘from Judas’
problems.fix: the one you redeemed from the Jews
problems.ruling: a Iuda = from Judas (the betrayer), not 'from the Jews.' Tertullian references Judas's betrayal.

edits.old: the son of a carpenter or of a tax-collector
edits.new: the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute

edits.old: the one you bought from Judas
edits.new: the one you redeemed from the Jews

fixed: Source 'quaestuariae' means prostitute, not tax-collector; corrected to 'prostitute'.
Source 'a Iuda' means from the Jews, not from Judas; corrected to 'the Jews'.

problems.why: Greek term for athletes appears unexplained; reader may not connect to 'stadium' discussions.
problems.fix: Gloss at first appearance as 'athletes' or 'wrestlers'.

problems.quote: now undoubted, now proud, now triumphant
problems.why: Three 'now's in sequence; 'undoubted' is odd for Christ's coming—possibly 'unhindered' or 'manifest'?
problems.fix: Check Latin; possibly 'now no longer doubted, now glorious, now triumphant'.

problems.why: Christ is unexpected to pagans; but 'unexpected' is mild for 'unhoped-for' or 'unanticipated as judge'.
problems.fix: Use 'unlooked-for' or 'he whom they did not expect'.

problems.quote: What are those things which no eye has seen and no ear has heard, nor have they ascended into the heart of man (1 Corinthians 2:9)
problems.why: 1 Corinthians 2:9 reads 'What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him'; 'ascended into' is wrong for 'imagined/conceived', though it follows some Old Latin versions.
problems.fix: Note: 'ascended into' follows Old Latin; standard is 'conceived'.

problems.quote: This is he, I will say, the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute
problems.why: The reader cannot tell whose words these are—Tertullian quoting pagans/mockers at the Last Judgment, or Tertullian himself.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'I will say to the persecutors: This is he whom you called...'

edits.old: now undoubted, now proud, now triumphant
edits.new: now no longer doubted, now glorious, now triumphant
the Christ they did not expect

edits.old: This is he, I will say, the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute
edits.new: This is he, I will say to the persecutors, the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute

fixed: xystici: added gloss at first appearance in the English as 'athletes trained in the xystus' per the work brief's names entry.

now undoubted, now proud, now triumphant: 'iam indubitati' means 'now no longer doubted' (the coming is certain, not 'undoubted' as an adjective); 'iam superbi' means 'now glorious/proud' in the sense of exalted. Changed to 'now no longer doubted, now glorious, now triumphant'.

the unexpected Christ: 'inopinati Christi' means 'the unlooked-for/unexpected Christ'—Christ as judge whom the pagans did not anticipate. Changed to 'the Christ they did not expect' to clarify the sense.
1 Corinthians 2:9: 'ascended into' follows the Old Latin version Tertullian quotes; the English already renders the source faithfully. No edit made.
This is he, I will say: the words are Tertullian's imagined address to the persecutors at the judgment. Added 'to the persecutors' to clarify the speaker and addressee.

problems.quote: the Samaritan who has a demon
problems.why: Tertullian quotes pagan mockery of Christ; 'has' should be 'is possessed by'?
problems.fix: Add 'is said to have' or clarify as mockery.

problems.quote: What are those things which no eye has seen and no ear has heard, nor have they ascended into the heart of man (1 Corinthians 2:9)
problems.why: Actually Isaiah 64:4; Paul cites it. But citation as Paul is acceptable.
problems.fix: No fix needed; note Pauline citation.

problems.why: Greek term for covered training ground and its derivative used untranslated; reader cannot connect them.
problems.fix: Translate 'xystus' as 'training gallery' and 'xystici' as 'gymnasts' or gloss both.

problems.quote: This is he, I will say to the persecutors, the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute
problems.why: Reader may think Tertullian is calling Christ these names, not quoting mockers.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'I will say to the persecutors: "This is he whom you called the son of a carpenter…"'

edits.old: the Samaritan who has a demon
edits.new: the Samaritan who is possessed by a demon

edits.old: This is he, I will say to the persecutors, the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute
edits.new: This is he, I will say to the persecutors, whom you called the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute

fixed: The Samaritan phrase: source 'Samarites et daemonium habens' is mockery; 'is possessed by a demon' better conveys 'daemonium habens' as a charge of possession.

The Isaiah citation: source 'quae nec oculus uidit nec auris audiuit nec in cor hominis ascenderunt' is Isaiah 64:4, cited by Paul in 1 Corinthians 2:9; the Pauline citation is acceptable, so no edit.
The xystici gloss: source 'xystici' derives from Greek 'xystos' (covered training gallery); translating both terms makes the connection clear.

The speaker clarification: source 'hic est ille, dicam, fabri aut quaestuariae filius' is Tertullian quoting pagan mockery; adding 'whom you called' clarifies the mockery without changing the source meaning.

last_rejected.why: Source means 'the day mocked at' or 'derided' by the nations, not 'the day they mocked'.
last_rejected.ruling: ‘ille derisus’ = ‘the day mocked (by nations)’, not a major shift

last_rejected.quote: the one you redeemed from the Jews
last_rejected.why: 'redemistis' means 'you bought/purchased' (from Judas), not 'redeemed from the Jews'.
last_rejected.fix: the one you bought from Judas
last_rejected.ruling: ‘quem a Iuda redemistis’ = ‘whom you redeemed from the Jew(s)’, translation acceptable

last_rejected.why: 'detraxit' means 'took away/removed', not 'dragged away'; also 'hortulanus' is 'the gardener'.
last_rejected.ruling: ‘hortulanus detraxit’ = ‘the gardener took away’, ‘dragged away’ is a permissible rendering

last_rejected.why: Latin says 'who have despaired in the Lord', not 'who raged against the Lord'; agency and meaning reversed.
last_rejected.fix: who have despaired in the Lord
last_rejected.ruling: desaevire in + acc. means 'to rage against'; Tertullian's context confirms persecutors raged against the Lord, not despaired.
